To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) fingerprint recognition accuracy is stable for children between 0-4, 2) fingerprint matching accuracy is similar for children in the 0-2 and 3-4 age groups and 3) fingerprint matching accuracy does not vary significantly with the number of fingerprints available for comparison (i.e., the more the number of fingerprint samples, the better the accuracy)
(a) fingerprint recognition accuracy is high for 0-4-year-old children; and (b) fingerprint recognition accuracy does not deteriorate with age, at least for children in the 0-2 years age group.

(1) the persistence of fingerprint matching for 0-4-year-old children is high, (2) the persistence of matching accuracy is not affected by age of the child, (3) the persistence of recognition accuracy for children aged 0-4 months is higher compared to children aged 4-12 months, 1-2 years and 2-4 years, (4) children aged 2-4 months and 1-2 months are easier to enroll than other children

fingerprint recognition accuracy for 0-4-year old children is comparable to that for adults, with the recognition accuracy being stable for at least 6 months.
fingerprint recognition is a promising biometric modality for children.
fingerprints are a viable biometric modality for recognition of 4 year-old children and possibly for 3 year-olds as well.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the persistence of biometrics for infants is not a trivial issue and requires a systematic approach.
fingerprint recognition for infants and toddlers is not only possible but also persistent over time, even when children do not follow instructions and are not cooperative.

the temporal persistence of biometric modalities for children in the 0-4 age group is a complex function of several factors, including the biometric modality, the child's age, the number of days since the last enrollment session, the child's gender, and the child's cooperation.
